# Threat model — what breaks this

Every failure rate below is measured, not estimated. Reproduce with:

    uv run python bench/adversarial/run_adversarial.py --all

## The weakest link

**Anchor evasion.** A judge change confined to a region your anchor set does not cover is
invisible, and Benchlock will attribute the resulting movement to your system — a
confident, wrong rollback recommendation. Stratified selection and coverage warnings make
it less likely. Nothing makes it go away.

If you take one thing from this document: **coverage is measured, never guaranteed**, and a
`SYSTEM` verdict is only as trustworthy as the anchor set's coverage of the ways your judge
could change.

## Summary

| attack | what it does | Benchlock's failure rate |
|---|---|---:|
| 7.1 anchor evasion | a judge change confined to a region the anchor set does not cover | **100%** |
| 7.4 anchor staleness | the team's own standard changed; frozen anchors read it as judge drift | **100%** |
| 7.5 input distribution shift | the eval suite itself moves, adding a third cause benchlock cannot model | **100%** |
| 7.9 provider-side response caching | a cached judge returns yesterday's answers, hiding real drift | **100%** |
| 7.3 cancellation | judge and system moving in opposite directions; the net score is flat | **25%** |
| 7.2 slow ramp | drift introduced gradually, below the per-run detectable threshold | **20%** |
| 7.6 adversarial ordering | worst-case ordering of observations within each run | **0%** |
| 7.7 heavy tails and bound violations | near-degenerate score distributions and out-of-range scores | **0%** |

A failure rate of 0% means the attack does not work against this design, and each section
says *why* rather than claiming a defence. A rate of 100% means it works reliably.

---

## 7.1 anchor evasion

**Measured failure rate: 100%.** WORKS — the fundamental limitation of the design; measured, warned about, never eliminated

**This is the weakest link in the design, and nothing in this document should be read as
softening it.**

A judge that changes its behaviour only within a region your anchor set does not cover is
invisible to the anchor stream. The system stream moves, the anchor stream does not, and
Benchlock returns `SYSTEM` — a confident rollback recommendation for a system that never
changed. That is the exact failure the tool exists to prevent, produced by the tool itself.

The measured curve of misattribution against anchor coverage is in
`bench/results/adversarial-latest.json`, and it is what sets the coverage warning threshold.

*What is done about it:* stratified selection guarantees at least one anchor per occupied
score decile and tag, and coverage is measured and warned about at baseline.
*What is not done about it:* nothing makes it go away. Coverage over the dimensions you
thought to tag says nothing about the dimensions you did not — response length, language,
whether the answer contains code. **Coverage is measured. It is never guaranteed.**

## 7.4 anchor staleness

**Measured failure rate: 100%.** WORKS BY CONSTRUCTION — benchlock reports *that* the judge changed, never *why*. A deliberate rubric change is indistinguishable from provider drift, and `benchlock rebaseline --reason` is the intended answer

Your own standard changed. Hedging used to be penalised; now it is fine, so you updated the
rubric. The judge is genuinely different, `frozen-self` anchors correctly report a judge
change — and what you wanted to hear was "your rubric changed", not "the judge drifted".

Benchlock reports **that** the judge moved, never **why**. A deliberate rubric edit and a
silent provider rotation are indistinguishable to it, and no amount of statistics will
separate them, because they are the same event as far as the measurement is concerned.

*What is done about it:* `benchlock rebaseline --reason rubric-updated` is the intended
answer, and the reason is recorded in the ledger and named in every subsequent verdict.
*What is not done about it:* the tool cannot tell you which it was. This is a limitation,
not a defect.

## 7.5 input distribution shift

**Measured failure rate: 100%.** PARTIALLY DEFENDED. When the item set changes, the suite-hash check refuses 100% of the time. When the ids stay the same and only the questions behind them get harder, the check is blind and 100% become a confident `system` verdict. Hashing item ids does not hash item content, and a fixed suite is an assumption benchlock states but cannot verify

The suite hash is a hash of item **ids**, not item **content**.

A suite whose 200 test slots are regenerated each month from production traffic keeps its
ids, keeps its hash, and changes completely underneath. Lattice rule 2 sees nothing, the
scores drop because the questions got harder, and the drop is attributed to the system.

*What is done about it:* when the item set genuinely changes, the suite-hash check refuses
to attribute, and that refusal is measured.
*What is not done about it:* an id-preserving content change is undefended. Hashing content
would defend it, at the cost of storing or hashing eval content that Hard Rule 9 keeps out
of the ledger — a trade-off not yet made. **A fixed suite is an assumption Benchlock states
but cannot fully verify.**

## 7.9 provider-side response caching

**Measured failure rate: 100%.** WORKS AGAINST THE SHIPPED DEFAULT, defensible by configuration. `judge.cache_busting_nonce` is FALSE unless you set it, so the 100% failure rate above is the out-of-the-box behaviour, not a hypothetical: drift visible in 0/20 runs without the nonce, 20/20 with it. Turning it on defends the attack completely in this simulation. NOTE: the nonce's measured effect on the mean score here is 0.0000, but that is an artefact of the simulated judge, whose nonce touches only the cache key. Whether a nonce perturbs a REAL judge's scores is UNMEASURED: Tier 2 used a nonce on every replicate call but never scored the same items with and without one, so the mitigation's own confounding effect is an open question rather than a verified non-issue

If your provider serves a cached response for an identical prompt, the anchor set returns
*yesterday's answers*. The anchor stream looks perfectly stable, real judge drift becomes
invisible, and the tool fails silently in the one direction it must not.

*What is done about it:* `judge.cache_busting_nonce: true` puts a per-run nonce in the
anchor prompt. With caching simulated, drift is invisible without it and fully visible with
it.
*What is not yet known:* whether the nonce itself perturbs a real judge's scores. Against
the built-in simulated judge the effect is exactly zero, but that is an artefact of the
simulation — the nonce there touches only a cache key. **A mitigation that is itself a
confound is not a mitigation, and this one is unverified against a real judge.**

## 7.3 cancellation

**Measured failure rate: 25%.** PARTIALLY DEFENDED — the difference-in-differences process sees it where a single stream cannot, but a small enough cancellation is still missed

The judge got stricter while the system improved by the same amount. The net eval score is
perfectly flat. Every single-stream detector sees a healthy pipeline.

*What is done about it:* the corrected stream is monitored as its own difference-in-
differences e-process, which is exactly the quantity that did *not* cancel. This is why
lattice rule 4 does not require the raw system stream to have crossed — the spec's literal
rule returns `STABLE` here.
*What remains:* a small enough cancellation is still missed. The measured miss rate by
effect size is in the results file.

## 7.2 slow ramp

**Measured failure rate: 20%.** WORKS below ~0.001 per run. 1 of 5 tested ramp rates were never detected within the horizon. A ramp slower than the noise floor is invisible to every method, this one included; the boundary is the useful number

Drift introduced gradually, below the per-run detectable threshold.

A ramp slower than the noise floor is invisible to every method, this one included. The
useful number is not "does it work" but *where the boundary is*, and that boundary is
measured rather than asserted.

## 7.6 adversarial ordering

**Measured failure rate: 0%.** NEGLIGIBLE — median delay penalty +0.0 runs. The stream is monitored at run level, so within-run ordering cannot starve the bets

Worst-case ordering of observations within a run, to starve a betting process of evidence.

This cannot work against this design, and it is worth saying why rather than claiming a
defence: the streams are monitored at **run level**, so the order of items *within* a run is
averaged away before the bets ever see it. The measured delay penalty is zero.

## 7.7 heavy tails and bound violations

**Measured failure rate: 0%.** DEFENDED — out-of-range scores are refused at ingest rather than clamped, and degenerate distributions produce a conservative verdict rather than a wrong one

Near-degenerate score distributions (99% at the ceiling), zero variance, and scores outside
their declared range.

Out-of-range scores are refused at ingest rather than clamped — clamping would compress
real movement into the bound and make a drifting stream look stable. Degenerate
distributions produce a conservative verdict rather than a wrong one.

## 7.8 A judge that got noisier without changing version

Should a judge whose *variance* rose — a provider-side inference change, a load-shedding
fallback to a smaller model — read as `JUDGE`?

**Benchlock's answer: not directly, and this is deliberate.**

The anchor process tests the judge's *mean*, against a null sized by the noise floor
measured at baseline. A pure increase in variance with an unchanged mean does not move that
test, so a noise spike alone does not produce a `judge` verdict.

The reasoning:

1. **A noisier judge is not a drifted judge.** The measurement got less precise; it did not
   move. Reporting `judge` would tell the team to re-baseline, which fixes nothing — the
   new baseline would be just as noisy.
2. **The consequence is already visible where it matters.** A noise floor measured before
   the spike is now too small, which makes the detector *more* likely to fire — and
   provisioning goes stale, so `min_detectable_judge_shift` is understated. The right
   response is to re-measure the floor, not to re-baseline the scores.
3. **Not silently, though.** A run whose anchor spread departs sharply from the measured
   floor is a signal in its own right, and surfacing it as a distinct warning — rather than
   folding it into the `judge` verdict — is the honest treatment.

*Status: the behaviour is deliberate and documented. A dedicated variance-change warning is
not implemented, and that gap is listed in the README's limitations rather than papered
over.*

## What is not in this model

- **A judge that is adversarial toward Benchlock specifically.** Benchlock assumes the
  judge is a measuring instrument that may drift, not an opponent that knows it is being
  watched.
- **A compromised ledger writer.** The hash chain is tamper-*evident*, not tamper-proof:
  someone who can rewrite the whole file can rewrite the whole chain. It defends against
  accidental corruption and casual editing, not against an attacker with write access.
- **Multi-judge ensembles and multi-suite portfolios.** One judge, one suite, one system.
